title: Gratitude and helping
hook: people made to feel grateful helped a stranger more (Bartlett and DeSteno, 2006)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the love hormone, with a question mark. Real hormone, overstated headlines. Did you catch an easy headline and ask what came after? Day one thousand three hundred sixteen.

The screen goes black. A long, dull task, nearly finished, and now the computer has frozen and it looks like the whole thing has to be done again. Then the person sitting next to you leans over, fiddles with a cable, and the work comes back. Relief, maybe, and something warmer than relief. That small scene wasn't an accident. It was staged, in a psychology lab, to make people feel grateful on purpose. What the researchers wanted to know came next: would that feeling change what people did for someone else?
screen: `THE SCREEN GOES BLACK.` → `A STRANGER FIXES IT.` → `STAGED, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. Monica Bartlett and David DeSteno arranged for a participant's computer to fail near the end of a tedious task. A partner, who was secretly part of the study, stepped in and fixed it, sparing them from starting over. Others went through the same session without being rescued. Second, the ask. Afterward, the participants were asked to help with an unpleasant survey that would take a while. Those who had been helped, and felt grateful, spent more time helping. Third, the surprising part. In one version of the study, the request came from a stranger, not from the person who had fixed the computer. Grateful people still helped more. So the gratitude wasn't only paying back a debt. It seemed to make people more willing to help, full stop. The researchers also checked that it wasn't just a good mood doing the work. Fourth, an old book that starts with thanks. Marcus Aurelius opens his Meditations not with a theory but with a list: what he learned from his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, his friends. Book one is, in large part, a record of debts to people. Much of what follows turns to how to live among others. This week has followed the same thread: being the one who helps, spending on someone else, kindness spreading, a softer voice inside, and two careful looks at big claims. Gratitude sits near the start of that chain. Something good comes in, and it moves toward the next person. Pass it on.
screen: `A STAGED RESCUE.` · `GRATEFUL PEOPLE HELPED LONGER.` · `EVEN WHEN A STRANGER ASKED.` · then, large: `A BOOK THAT STARTS WITH THANKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a short list, the way Marcus began. Settle into the breath. Bring to mind one person who helped you, recently or long ago. Silently name what they gave you, as plainly as Marcus might: from this person, patience; from that one, a ride home on a bad night. Stay with that one person for a few breaths. If another comes, add them to the list. Then let the list rest, and notice the warmth that comes with it, or doesn't. Either way, keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
Gratitude and helping. In the lab, people who felt grateful helped more, even when a stranger asked. Today's word.
Your line: pass it on. Today, thank someone, then help someone, maybe a different person. Let the second follow the first. Day one thousand three hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Some people keep a regular gratitude practice, naming people or things they are thankful for, and some religious traditions build thanks into daily prayer. Some pair thanks with a small act of help.

original.note: Latin for "thanks," as in the Latin liturgy's reply Deo gratias, "thanks be to God."

trapdoor: what you thought: gratitude is a nice feeling you keep to yourself.
what it means: in the lab, feeling grateful made people more willing to help, even someone new.
what a scholar hears: Bartlett and DeSteno staged a rescue, then had a stranger ask for help; grateful participants still gave more time, and a good mood alone didn't explain it.

sources.ref: Bartlett and DeSteno, "Gratitude and prosocial behavior: helping when it costs you" (Psychological Science)

notes: Confirm the Bartlett and DeSteno details: a staged computer failure fixed by a confederate; helping measured as time spent on a tedious survey; a study in which a stranger made the request; and that positive mood alone did not account for the effect.
Week end (days 1310–1316): the teach looks back over the week in one sentence.
